## Bonn & Erlangen (Germany)

**Jürgen Schüttler** — anesthesiologist; propofol and opioid pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, population PK, and closed-loop anesthesia (University of Bonn, then chair at Erlangen)

Schüttler is one of the central figures in intravenous anesthetic PK/PD. With Schwilden and Stoeckel in Bonn he co-developed and validated EEG-driven closed-loop control of intravenous anesthetics and helped translate compartmental modeling into practical model-based infusion, collaborating with Donald Stanski's Stanford group on EEG measures of opioid and hypnotic drug effect. His most widely cited contribution is a large multicenter population pharmacokinetic analysis of propofol (with Harald Ihmsen), which quantified the influence of age, weight, and mode of administration on propofol disposition using a three-compartment model — parameters that underpin modern TCI systems. Across his career he also characterized the PK/PD of opioids (e.g., alfentanil, fentanyl) and their interaction with hypnotics, contributing to the response-surface understanding of anesthetic drug combinations.

*Key reference:* Schüttler J, Ihmsen H. Population pharmacokinetics of propofol: a multicenter study. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(3):727–738.

---

**Helmut Schwilden** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; pioneer of EEG-guided, model-based, and closed-loop intravenous anesthesia

Schwilden laid much of the quantitative groundwork for target-controlled infusion (TCI) and feedback-controlled anesthesia. His 1981 paper derived a general algorithm for computing the dosing regimen needed to reach and hold a desired drug concentration in any compartment of a linear pharmacokinetic model — the mathematical basis for the "BET" (bolus–elimination–transfer) infusion schemes later used in TCI. He then pursued the electroencephalogram (EEG) as a real-time pharmacodynamic measure of anesthetic drug effect, championing the median EEG frequency (and spectral edge frequency) as the controlled variable. Working with Hugo Stoeckel and Jürgen Schüttler in Bonn, he built and clinically tested adaptive closed-loop systems that titrated methohexital and propofol to a target median EEG frequency, among the first true closed-loop general-anesthesia demonstrations in humans. This EEG-and-pharmacokinetics program, developed in close collaboration with Schüttler and with Donald Stanski's group, helped establish the effect-site/ke0 framework linking plasma concentration to measurable CNS effect.

*Key references:* Schwilden H. A general method for calculating the dosage scheme in linear pharmacokinetics. Eur J Clin Pharmacol. 1981;20(5):379–386. • Schwilden H, Stoeckel H, Schüttler J. Closed-loop feedback control of propofol anaesthesia by quantitative EEG analysis in humans. Br J Anaesth. 1989;62(3):290–296.

---

## Brussels — Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), Belgium

**Frederic Camu** — emeritus professor and long-time chair of anesthesiology, Vrije Universiteit Brussel

Frederic Camu was a Belgian anesthesiologist who led the Department of Anesthesiology at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) for many years and built a research program centered on the clinical pharmacology of intravenous anesthetics, opioids, and analgesics — including their effects on hemodynamics, respiratory control, and acute nociception `[verify]`. Working at Brussels in the mid-1980s, he collaborated with Elisabeth Gepts on the human disposition studies of propofol that would become foundational to modern target-controlled infusion (TCI).

Camu was a co-author of the 1987 Gepts et al. constant-rate infusion study, whose three-compartment parameter set was later adapted by Marsh, White, Morton, and Kenny into the "Marsh" model used in the Diprifusor and many subsequent TCI systems, and against which Coetzee and colleagues benchmarked propofol model performance. Frederic Camu passed away in 2024.

*Key reference:* Gepts E, Camu F, Cockshott ID, Douglas EJ. Disposition of propofol administered as constant rate intravenous infusions in humans. Anesth Analg. 1987;66(12):1256–1263.

---

**Elisabeth Gepts** — clinical-pharmacology researcher in anesthesiology; source of the propofol disposition dataset underlying the Marsh model

Elisabeth Gepts (published as "Gepts E") was a Brussels-based clinical pharmacology and anesthesiology researcher whose 1987 study of propofol disposition during constant-rate intravenous infusion provided the parameter estimates that underpin one of the most widely deployed pharmacokinetic models in anesthesia. In that work she and colleagues administered propofol at 3, 6, and 9 mg·kg⁻¹·hr⁻¹ to surgical patients under regional anesthesia, sampled arterial blood during and after infusion, and fitted the data to a three-compartment open mammillary model with central elimination — establishing the volumes and clearances that describe propofol disposition in humans.

That dataset, produced through the Camu–Gepts collaboration at the Free University of Brussels, was subsequently adapted by Marsh, White, Morton, and Kenny (1991) into the weight-proportional "Marsh" model implemented in the AstraZeneca Diprifusor and in numerous later TCI pumps; it also served as a reference point in Coetzee et al.'s comparative evaluations of propofol PK models. Gepts is credited with later helping to recover the original source data underlying these parameters.

*Key reference:* Gepts E, Camu F, Cockshott ID, Douglas EJ. Disposition of propofol administered as constant rate intravenous infusions in humans. Anesth Analg. 1987;66(12):1256–1263.

---

## Duke University

**J. Michael Alvis** — biomedical engineer and anesthesiology investigator; principal developer of the CACI (computer-assisted continuous infusion) system

Michael Alvis was the engineer who, with J. Gerald Reves at Duke, built one of the first practical computer-assisted continuous infusion systems for intravenous anesthetics. The CACI system used a pharmacokinetic model of fentanyl to compute the infusion-rate schedule needed to rapidly reach and then hold a target plasma concentration, and to let the anesthesiologist raise or lower that target interactively during surgery. In a controlled comparison in cardiac surgical patients, the CACI method achieved and maintained target plasma fentanyl concentrations more reliably than skilled manual administration.

This work is widely regarded as a foundational proof of concept for target-controlled infusion. Alvis also described the interactive control system in the engineering literature, establishing the model-driven infusion architecture later refined into systems such as STANPUMP and the commercial "Diprifusor."

*Key references:* Alvis JM, Reves JG, Govier AV, Menkhaus PG, Henling CE, Spain JA, Bradley E. Computer-assisted continuous infusions of fentanyl during cardiac anesthesia: comparison with a manual method. Anesthesiology. 1985;63(1):41–49. • Alvis JM, Reves JG, Spain JA, Sheppard LC. Computer-assisted continuous infusion of the intravenous analgesic fentanyl during general anesthesia — an interactive system. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1985;32(5):323–329. `[verify: issue/pages]`

---

**Peter S. A. Glass** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; leader in target-controlled infusion research (Duke University, later Stony Brook)

Peter Glass is a leading clinical investigator of target-controlled infusion and of the pharmacology of short-acting anesthetic agents. He directed influential first-in-human and validation studies characterizing the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the ultra-short-acting opioid remifentanil, and he contributed extensively to the clinical validation of propofol and opioid TCI. His volunteer and surgical studies helped define the concentration–effect relationships that underpin practical target-controlled dosing.

Glass also co-authored the work that introduced the "context-sensitive half-time," a concept that reshaped how anesthesiologists reason about drug offset after continuous infusion. His body of work bridged rigorous PK/PD modeling and everyday clinical dosing decisions.

*Key reference:* Glass PSA, Hardman D, Kamiyama Y, Quill TJ, Marton G, Donn KH, Grosse CM, Hermann D. Preliminary pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of an ultra-short-acting opioid: remifentanil (GI87084B). Anesth Analg. 1993;77(5):1031–1040.

---

**James R. Jacobs** — biomedical engineer; developer of TCI control algorithms and co-originator of the context-sensitive half-time concept

James Jacobs made foundational engineering contributions to model-driven drug delivery in anesthesia. He derived an analytically optimal control algorithm for driving a pharmacokinetic model to a physician-specified target concentration, a formulation that made real-time, interactively adjustable target-controlled infusion practical and that influenced systems in the STANPUMP lineage. His later work extended targeting from the plasma to the effect site.

With Michael Hughes and Peter Glass, Jacobs introduced the context-sensitive half-time — the time for drug concentration to fall by 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration — demonstrating that the traditional elimination half-life poorly predicts recovery after anesthetic infusions and providing a clinically meaningful measure of drug offset.

*Key references:* Jacobs JR. Algorithm for optimal linear model-based control with application to pharmacokinetic model-driven drug delivery. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1990;37(1):107–109. • Hughes MA, Glass PSA, Jacobs JR. Context-sensitive half-time in multicompartment pharmacokinetic models for intravenous anesthetic drugs. Anesthesiology. 1992;76(3):334–341.

---

**J. Gerald "Jerry" Reves** — cardiac anesthesiologist; chair of anesthesiology at Duke, later dean of the College of Medicine at the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC)

Jerry Reves was a pioneer of modern cardiac anesthesia and a central mentor of the Duke group that developed computer-assisted continuous infusion (CACI). Trained at MUSC and the University of Alabama at Birmingham, he built the cardiac anesthesia division at Duke University, chaired the Department of Anesthesiology there (1991–2001), and served as dean and vice president for medical affairs at MUSC (2001–2010). His research established much of the clinical pharmacology of the benzodiazepine midazolam in anesthesia and advanced the understanding of opioid (fentanyl) pharmacokinetics during cardiac surgery.

Working with engineer J. Michael Alvis, Reves led the Duke effort that translated three-compartment pharmacokinetic models into a bedside infusion controller, producing the landmark 1985 demonstration that a computer-driven infusion could target and maintain a chosen plasma fentanyl concentration more accurately than manual bolus dosing. This work is a direct forerunner of contemporary target-controlled infusion (TCI) systems.

*Key references:* Reves JG, Fragen RJ, Vinik HR, Greenblatt DJ. Midazolam: pharmacology and uses. Anesthesiology. 1985;62(3):310–324. • Alvis JM, Reves JG, Govier AV, et al. Computer-assisted continuous infusions of fentanyl during cardiac anesthesia: comparison with a manual method. Anesthesiology. 1985;63(1):41–49.

---

## Emory University

**James M. Bailey** — anesthesiologist and PK/PD modeler; context-sensitive/decrement times and closed-loop control (Emory University; later Northeast Georgia)

Bailey applied rigorous pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling and simulation to questions of anesthetic onset and recovery. He is closely associated with the "context-sensitive half-time" concept — the time for drug concentration to fall 50% after stopping an infusion of a given duration — introduced for intravenous drugs by Hughes, Glass, and Jacobs (a group in the modeling tradition that also includes Steven Shafer). Bailey extended the idea to the inhaled anesthetics, using computer simulation to compute context-sensitive half-times and other decrement times (80%, 90%) for enflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, and desflurane, clarifying how duration of administration governs emergence. He also contributed to model-based and closed-loop drug delivery and to the general methodology of quantifying the time course of anesthetic drug effect.

*Key references:* Bailey JM. Context-sensitive half-times and other decrement times of inhaled anesthetics. Anesth Analg. 1997;85(3):681–686. • (Foundational related work: Hughes MA, Glass PSA, Jacobs JR. Context-sensitive half-time in multicompartment pharmacokinetic models for intravenous anesthetic drugs. Anesthesiology. 1992;76(3):334–341.)

---

**Carl C. Hug Jr.** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist; professor of anesthesiology and pharmacology

Carl Hug was a leading academic authority on the clinical pharmacology of the synthetic opioids used in anesthesia, particularly fentanyl and alfentanil. Holding both an MD and a PhD in pharmacology, he devoted nearly six decades to anesthesiology research and education at Emory. His studies helped establish the plasma concentration–effect relationships of opioids during surgery and the concept of alfentanil as a "kinetically predictable" analgesic well suited to infusion-based dosing.

Among his most cited work, the study with Ausems, Stanski, and Burm defined the plasma alfentanil concentrations required to blunt responses to specific surgical stimuli (intubation, incision, closure) during nitrous oxide anesthesia — data that directly informed rational opioid infusion regimens and TCI targets. Hug also held major leadership roles, serving as president of the American Board of Anesthesiology (1992–1993) and of the Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research (1998–2001). Carl Hug passed away in 2022.

*Key reference:* Ausems ME, Hug CC Jr, Stanski DR, Burm AGL. Plasma concentrations of alfentanil required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia for general surgery. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(4):362–373.

---

## FDA — U.S. Food and Drug Administration

**Carl C. Peck** — physician and clinical pharmacologist; first Director of the FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), 1987–1994 `[verify: 1993 vs 1994]`; founder of the Center for Drug Development Science

Carl Peck is among the most influential advocates for quantitative, model-based drug development and for embedding pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) and exposure-response reasoning into regulatory decision-making. Trained in internal medicine and clinical pharmacology, he directed the Division of Clinical Pharmacology at the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (1980–1987) before becoming the first Director of CDER when the FDA split its drug and biologics centers in 1987, and he led CDER until 1994.

At and after the FDA, Peck argued that drug development should be a structured, quantitative learning process rather than a series of isolated trials. Working alongside Lewis B. Sheiner and other pioneers of population PK/PD, he helped popularize the "learn and confirm" paradigm and pushed for exposure-response analysis, population modeling, and simulation as tools for dose selection and labeling — the same modeling tradition that underlies target-controlled infusion (TCI) and PK/PD models for anesthetics. In 1994 he founded the Center for Drug Development Science (CDDS) at Georgetown University Medical Center, later affiliated with the UCSF School of Pharmacy. He received the ASCPT Sheiner–Beal Pharmacometrics Award in 2017.

*Key reference:* Peck CC, Barr WH, Benet LZ, et al. Opportunities for integration of pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and toxicokinetics in rational drug development. Pharm Res. 1992;9(6):826–833.

---

**Daniel A. Spyker** — physician-engineer (PhD, MD) and pharmacokineticist; academic clinical pharmacology (University of Virginia), later FDA medical officer (CDER)

Daniel Spyker combines formal quantitative training with clinical medicine: a PhD in electrical engineering and mathematics and an MD, with board certifications in internal medicine, medical toxicology, and clinical pharmacology `[verify]`. For roughly a decade he served on the internal-medicine faculty in the Division of Clinical Pharmacology at the University of Virginia, where he helped build the Blue Ridge Poison Center and applied compartmental modeling and Bayesian pharmacokinetic methods to dosing and poisoning problems — bridging rigorous PK analysis with clinical toxicology and poison-control practice.

His early research produced quantitative pharmacokinetic studies of antibiotics, including dose-dependent (nonlinear) absorption of amoxicillin across intravenous, oral, and intramuscular routes — work still cited in modern analyses of amoxicillin absorption kinetics. He later served as a Medical Officer in FDA's CDER (Pilot Drug Evaluation Staff), contributing to pharmacokinetics, exposure-response, and dose/exposure evaluation in the review setting, and subsequently worked in the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH). His career reflects the same emphasis on quantitative clinical pharmacology and model-based analysis that characterizes the PK/PD tradition used in anesthetic simulation.

*Key reference:* Spyker DA, Rugloski RJ, Vann RL, O'Brien WM. Pharmacokinetics of amoxicillin: dose dependence after intravenous, oral, and intramuscular administration. Antimicrob Agents Chemother. 1977;11(1):132–141.

---

## Ghent University & Demed Engineering (Belgium)

**Tom De Smet** — biomedical engineer; developer of RUGLOOP/TOOLBOX TCI software; founder of Demed Engineering, Temse (Belgium)

De Smet is the biomedical engineer who, with Michel Struys at Ghent University, built the RUGLOOP modular TCI and closed-loop software (later succeeded by TOOLBOX) that underpinned much of the Ghent group's TCI and automated-anesthesia research. The software captured physiologic monitor data and implemented both open-loop TCI and BIS-guided closed-loop control of propofol. He is associated with the medical-engineering firm Demed (Temse, Belgium) and is a co-owner of the RUGLOOP software.

His methodological contributions include simulation-based performance evaluation of closed-loop controllers and the development of a Bayesian-based, patient-individualized adaptive control method for BIS-guided propofol delivery, validated for clinical feasibility.

*Key reference:* De Smet T, Struys MMRF, Neckebroek MM, Van den Hauwe K, Bonte S, Mortier EP. The accuracy and clinical feasibility of a new bayesian-based closed-loop control system for propofol administration using the bispectral index as a controlled variable. Anesth Analg. 2008;107(4):1200–1210.

---

## Harvard Medical School — Boston (MGH & Brigham and Women's Hospital)

**James H. Philip** — anesthesiologist and bioengineer, Brigham and Women's Hospital; author of the "Gas Man" simulation `[verify: you wrote "James Philips"; correct name is "James H. Philip"]`

James H. Philip is an anesthesiologist and bioengineer who created "Gas Man," the widely used educational program that simulates the uptake and distribution of inhaled anesthetics. Gas Man depicts, pictorially and graphically, the movement of anesthetic gas and vapor from the vaporizer through the breathing circuit, lungs, blood, and tissues to the site of action in the brain and spinal cord, and models agents including halothane, enflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, nitrous oxide, xenon, and ether. First developed in the 1980s and refined over decades, it remains a standard teaching tool for inhalation-anesthesia kinetics.

Philip's broader contributions span anesthesia pharmacokinetic simulation, gas and vapor monitoring, and clinical instrumentation, complementing the closely related monitoring and infusion work of colleagues such as Daniel Raemer at the neighboring Harvard hospitals.

*Key reference:* Philip JH. Gas Man — an example of goal-oriented computer-assisted teaching which results in learning. Int J Clin Monit Comput. 1986;3(3):165–173.

---

**Daniel B. Raemer** — biomedical engineer, Massachusetts General Hospital; gas monitoring, model-driven infusion, and anesthesia simulation

Dan Raemer is a bioengineer (PhD) whose early work centered on respiratory gas monitoring and capnography and on the instrumentation and control of drug delivery. He was a key contributor to model-driven (target-controlled) drug infusion, applying population pharmacokinetics prospectively to computer-controlled infusion pumps so that a desired plasma or effect-site concentration could be targeted rather than a fixed infusion rate — a foundational validation for the class of tools that simulators like stanpumpR embody. This work was carried out with S. L. Shafer, J. R. Varvel, and colleagues.

In the second phase of his career Raemer became a founder of modern anesthesia patient simulation, helping establish the Center for Medical Simulation (Harvard) and serving as the founding president of the Society for Simulation in Healthcare (2005). He held appointments as a bioengineer at MGH and Associate Professor of Anaesthesia at Harvard Medical School.

*Key reference:* Raemer DB, Buschman A, Varvel JR, Philip BK, Johnson MD, Stein DA, Shafer SL. The prospective use of population pharmacokinetics in a computer-driven infusion system for alfentanil. Anesthesiology. 1990;73(1):66–72.

---

**Carl E. Rosow** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist, Massachusetts General Hospital

Carl Rosow was a clinician-scientist who bridged anesthesiology and pharmacology, holding both an MD and a PhD in pharmacology (Boston University). For over three decades at MGH and Harvard Medical School he taught anesthetic pharmacology and conducted clinical studies of opioid pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. His early work on opioid-induced histamine release helped explain the hemodynamic differences among morphine, fentanyl, and related agents, informing safer intraoperative opioid use.

With colleagues and mentees — notably Mark Dershwitz — Rosow carried out clinical pharmacology studies of newer agents including butorphanol, sufentanil, ondansetron, and remifentanil, and contributed to the understanding of opioid–hypnotic interactions and measures of drug effect such as MAC-awake. He was widely regarded as a clinical authority on anesthetic drug behavior. Carl Rosow passed away in 2021.

*Key reference:* Rosow CE, Moss J, Philbin DM, Savarese JJ. Histamine release during morphine and fentanyl anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1982;56(2):93–96.

---

## ICI / Zeneca / AstraZeneca (industry, United Kingdom)

**John Baird "Iain" Glen** — veterinarian and pharmacologist; discoverer of propofol (Diprivan) and leader of the Diprifusor TCI program

Glen — a Scottish veterinary surgeon by training, who publishes and is widely known as "Iain" (formal name John Baird Glen) — identified propofol (2,6-diisopropylphenol) as an anesthetic while working at Imperial Chemical Industries beginning in the early 1970s, and led its development into the clinically used formulation Diprivan. He subsequently coordinated the development of the "Diprifusor," the first commercial target-controlled infusion system for propofol, including assessment of delivery performance and collaboration with pump manufacturers. For the discovery and development of propofol he received the 2018 Lasker–DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award.

*Key reference:* Glen JB. The development of 'Diprifusor': a TCI system for propofol. Anaesthesia. 1998;53(Suppl 1):13–21. `[verify: page range]`

---

## Leiden University Medical Center (Netherlands)

**M. E. Ausems** — anesthesiologist; alfentanil pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics and model-based ("computer-assisted") infusion `[verify: first name — the help page lists "Max"; publications use initials "M. E. Ausems"]`

Ausems carried out foundational work defining the plasma alfentanil concentrations required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia and to suppress responses to specific surgical stimuli, translating opioid effect into concentration targets that could be actively controlled. This research was a direct precursor to modern target-controlled infusion (TCI): it established the concentration–effect relationships that a model-based infusion device must aim for. The doctoral work was based at the University of Leiden `[verify: dates]`.

Ausems collaborated with Carl C. Hug Jr., Donald R. Stanski, and Anton G. L. Burm — a partnership spanning the Leiden and U.S. (Emory/Stanford) pharmacology groups — and subsequently compared computer-assisted (target-controlled) infusion against intermittent bolus administration of alfentanil, helping to demonstrate that model-driven infusion produces more stable and predictable opioid concentrations.

*Key reference:* Ausems ME, Hug CC Jr, Stanski DR, Burm AGL. Plasma concentrations of alfentanil required to supplement nitrous oxide anesthesia for general surgery. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(4):362–373.

---

**James G. Bovill** — anesthesiologist; Professor of Anaesthesia, Leiden University Medical Center (1985–2007 `[verify]`); opioid PK/PD in cardiac anesthesia

Bovill, trained in Belfast, was a leading figure in intravenous and cardiac anesthesia and a driving force behind the Leiden opioid PK/PD program. His early work established the pharmacokinetics of high-dose fentanyl in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, including the effect of cardiopulmonary bypass on plasma concentrations, and he extended this to comparative studies of fentanyl, sufentanil, and alfentanil in cardiac and valvular surgery. With Peter Sebel and others he correlated opioid dosing with electroencephalographic (EEG) measures of drug effect, an important step toward quantitative opioid pharmacodynamics.

As department head at Leiden, Bovill fostered the intravenous-anesthesia group whose propofol–opioid interaction and TCI research (Vuyk, Engbers, Burm) became internationally influential; he is a co-author on the landmark Vuyk interaction studies. His opioid PK/PD work fed directly into the effect-compartment and TCI modeling that underlies systems developed in the broader community.

*Key references:* Bovill JG, Sebel PS. Pharmacokinetics of high-dose fentanyl: a study in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Br J Anaesth. 1980;52(8):795–801. • Bovill JG, Sebel PS, Stanley TH. Opioid analgesics in anesthesia: with special reference to their use in cardiovascular anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 1984;61(6):731–755.

---

**Anton G. L. Burm** — clinical pharmacologist, Department of Anaesthesiology, Leiden University Medical Center (LUMC)

Burm was the clinical-pharmacology anchor of the Leiden intravenous-anesthesia group, specializing in the pharmacokinetics of local anesthetics and opioids. He pioneered the use of stable-isotope (deuterium-labelled) methods to separate systemic absorption from disposition after epidural and subarachnoid administration: by giving a labelled analogue intravenously at the moment of neuraxial dosing, he could resolve the two processes from a single set of plasma samples — work he later extended to the effect of age on bupivacaine absorption and disposition. He also characterized the stereoselective (enantiomer-specific) pharmacokinetics of bupivacaine, showing that the R- and S-enantiomers differ in disposition after intravenous administration of the racemate, foundational to the later clinical adoption of levobupivacaine and ropivacaine.

Within the Leiden group, Burm was a recurring co-author on the propofol–opioid interaction and TCI studies led by Vuyk and Bovill, contributing pharmacokinetic modeling and assay expertise. His methods connect to the wider PK/PD community that produced the target-controlled infusion models used in tools such as STANPUMP.

*Key references:* Burm AG, van der Meer AD, van Kleef JW, Zeijlmans PW, Groen K. Pharmacokinetics of the enantiomers of bupivacaine following intravenous administration of the racemate. Br J Clin Pharmacol. 1994;38(2):125–129. • Burm AGL, van Kleef JW, Vermeulen NPE, Olthof G, Breimer DD, Spierdijk J. Pharmacokinetics of lignocaine and bupivacaine in surgical patients following epidural administration: simultaneous investigation of absorption and disposition kinetics using stable isotopes. Clin Pharmacokinet. 1987;13(3):191–203. `[verify: exact pages]`

---

**Frank H. M. Engbers** — anesthesiologist (now retired), Leiden University Medical Center; clinical implementation of target-controlled infusion

Engbers is a clinician-implementer of target-controlled infusion, focused on making TCI and effect-site targeting practical, safe, and teachable at the bedside. He co-authored the Leiden propofol–alfentanil interaction studies (providing the TCI delivery), and he became a widely cited authority on the clinical behavior of TCI systems — the proliferation of pharmacokinetic models in open TCI pumps, the pitfalls of extrapolating anthropometric data, effect-site ("effect-compartment") steering, and the regulatory ambiguities of TCI practice. His analyses of TCI "anomalies" after two decades of clinical use are standard reading for understanding why different pumps and models can produce different infusions for the same target.

Engbers has also been central to TCI education and simulation, associated with teaching/driver software such as RugLoop and TivaTrainer that let clinicians visualize plasma and effect-site concentrations `[verify: exact software roles]`. His clinical-implementation perspective links the Leiden group to the broader TCI community and to the ongoing standardization of TCI models.

*Key reference:* Engbers FHM, Dahan A. Anomalies in target-controlled infusion: an analysis after 20 years of clinical use. Anaesthesia. 2018;73(5):619–630. `[verify: full co-author list]`

---

**Jaap Vuyk** — anesthesiologist, Leiden University Medical Center; propofol–opioid interaction and response-surface modeling

Vuyk is best known for defining the pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and opioids and translating it into rational dosing. Using computer-controlled (target-controlled) infusion of both drugs, his Leiden studies quantified how propofol reduces alfentanil requirements and how alfentanil lowers the propofol concentration at which patients wake, mapping the synergy across clinical endpoints. He then advanced response-surface / concentration-pair modeling to identify the optimal EC50–EC95 propofol–opioid concentration combinations that provide adequate anesthesia while assuring the most rapid return of consciousness — the conceptual basis for interaction-guided TCI dosing and a direct antecedent of the interaction facets used in modern PK/PD tools.

This work was performed with the Leiden group (Engbers, Burm, Bovill, Olofsen, Mertens) and connects closely to the wider TCI and interaction-modeling community (Shafer/STANPUMP; Minto and Schnider's response-surface methods; Struys' closed-loop and TCI research). Vuyk's optimal-concentration framework remains a standard reference for combining hypnotics and opioids.

*Key references:* Vuyk J, Lim T, Engbers FH, Burm AG, Vletter AA, Bovill JG. The pharmacodynamic interaction of propofol and alfentanil during lower abdominal surgery in women. Anesthesiology. 1995;83(1):8–22. • Vuyk J, Mertens MJ, Olofsen E, Burm AG, Bovill JG. Propofol anesthesia and rational opioid selection: determination of optimal EC50–EC95 propofol–opioid concentrations that assure adequate anesthesia and a rapid return of consciousness. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(6):1549–1562.

## Northwestern University

**Michael J. Avram** — pharmacologist/analytical chemist; recirculatory pharmacokinetic modeling and precise marker kinetics (Feinberg School of Medicine)

Michael Avram is a pharmacologist at Northwestern University whose analytical rigor and quantitative modeling anchored the department's recirculatory pharmacokinetics program. His high-precision assay methods — resolving indocyanine green, thiopental, antipyrine, and other markers and drugs in arterial samples drawn at few-second intervals — made it possible to characterize the earliest, fastest phase of drug disposition after intravenous injection. With his long-standing collaborator Thomas Krejcie (and Thomas Henthorn), Avram built recirculatory models that decompose early kinetics into circulatory mixing, first-pass pulmonary uptake, and rapid peripheral distribution, using co-administered markers of blood, extracellular fluid, and total body water.

This body of work reframed how the onset of rapidly acting anesthetics is understood: front-end kinetics, driven by cardiac output and mixing, determine the arterial and effect-site concentration profile in the critical first minutes, informing bolus dosing strategy and the physiologic basis of plasma-to-effect-site equilibration used in TCI.

*Key references:* Avram MJ, Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK. The relationship of age to the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution: the concurrent disposition of thiopental and indocyanine green. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):403–411. • Krejcie TC, Avram MJ. What determines anesthetic induction dose? It's the front-end kinetics, doctor! Anesth Analg. 1999;89(3):541–544. `[verify: volume/page]`

---

**Thomas K. Henthorn** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; recirculatory/physiologic PK and front-end kinetics (Northwestern University; later Professor and Chair of Anesthesiology, University of Colorado `[verify: chair]`)

Thomas Henthorn trained at Northwestern University, where he was part of the recirculatory-modeling collaboration with Thomas Krejcie and Michael Avram, and he later moved to the University of Colorado, where he is Professor of Anesthesiology (and Adjoint Professor of Pharmaceutical Sciences). His research centers on the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution, physiologically based and recirculatory modeling, and the disposition of markers such as indocyanine green, with continued interests in drug transporters, metabolism, and pharmacogenetics.

Within the Northwestern program, Henthorn contributed to models that resolve the first-pass and rapid-distribution phase governing the onset of intravenous anesthetics and opioids. This front-end kinetic work clarifies how circulatory mixing and pulmonary uptake shape the arterial concentration profile immediately after injection — the phase most relevant to bolus dosing and to effect-site targeting in modern anesthetic delivery.

*Key references:* Avram MJ, Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK. The relationship of age to the pharmacokinetics of early drug distribution: the concurrent disposition of thiopental and indocyanine green. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):403–411. • Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK, Shanks CA, Avram MJ. A recirculatory pharmacokinetic model describing the circulatory mixing, tissue distribution and elimination of antipyrine in dogs. J Pharmacol Exp Ther. 1994;269(2):609–616.

**Thomas C. Krejcie** — anesthesiologist; recirculatory ("front-end") pharmacokinetic modeling of early drug distribution (Feinberg School of Medicine)

Thomas Krejcie is an anesthesiologist at Northwestern University whose research, in close and long-standing collaboration with pharmacologist Michael J. Avram, established the recirculatory (front-end) approach to pharmacokinetics. Where classical compartmental models begin describing a drug only after blood-sampling "mixing," Krejcie and colleagues sampled arterial blood every few seconds after injection to characterize the first minutes of disposition — the circulatory mixing, first-pass pulmonary uptake, and rapid tissue distribution that determine the onset of rapidly acting IV drugs. Their models used simultaneously administered markers of intravascular space (indocyanine green), extracellular fluid, and total body water, together with anesthetic and analgesic drugs such as thiopental and fentanyl, to partition early kinetics into physiologically interpretable elements.

This front-end perspective is directly relevant to bolus and infusion behavior of anesthetics: it explains why peak effect-site concentration and time-to-peak depend on cardiac output and mixing, informing rational bolus dosing and the plasma–effect-site (ke0) relationships used in TCI. Krejcie collaborated closely with Avram and with Thomas Henthorn on this Northwestern recirculatory-model program.

*Key reference:* Krejcie TC, Henthorn TK, Shanks CA, Avram MJ. A recirculatory pharmacokinetic model describing the circulatory mixing, tissue distribution and elimination of antipyrine in dogs. J Pharmacol Exp Ther. 1994;269(2):609–616.

## Stanford University

**Thomas W. Bouillon** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist; research fellow with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford (later University of Bern and the pharmaceutical industry); response-surface modeling of the propofol–remifentanil interaction

Thomas Bouillon is an anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist whose work centers on the quantitative PK/PD of intravenous anesthetics. As a research fellow in Steven L. Shafer's laboratory at Stanford, he became a leading contributor to response-surface modeling of the propofol–remifentanil interaction, characterizing how a hypnotic and an opioid combine across the full range of clinically relevant effect-site concentrations rather than at isolated dose pairs. His landmark 2004 study quantified the interaction for multiple endpoints simultaneously — hypnosis (no response to shaking and shouting), tolerance of laryngoscopy, and the processed-EEG measures bispectral index (BIS) and approximate entropy — demonstrating marked synergy for the clinical endpoints while the EEG measures behaved more additively. This work is a cornerstone of modern effect-site-targeted, interaction-aware anesthetic dosing.

Bouillon also made foundational contributions to modeling opioid-induced ventilatory depression, applying indirect-effect (non–steady-state) models to arterial and end-tidal CO2 during and after remifentanil administration — quantifying the potency and time course of respiratory depression and underscoring the hazard of bolus dosing of fast-onset opioids in spontaneously breathing patients. After his Stanford fellowship he worked in Switzerland (University of Bern / Inselspital, with Thomas Schnider's group) and subsequently moved into the pharmaceutical industry as a pharmacometrician (including at Novartis, Basel). `[verify: birth year; exact Stanford and Bern dates]`

*Key references:* Bouillon TW, Bruhn J, Radulescu L, Andresen C, Shafer TJ, Cohane C, Shafer SL. Pharmacodynamic interaction between propofol and remifentanil regarding hypnosis, tolerance of laryngoscopy, bispectral index, and electroencephalographic approximate entropy. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1353–1372. • Bouillon T, Bruhn J, Radu-Radulescu L, Andresen C, Cohane C, Shafer SL. A model of the ventilatory depressant potency of remifentanil in the non–steady state. Anesthesiology. 2003;99(4):779–787.

**Pedro L. Gambús** — anesthesiologist; research fellow in the Stanford/Palo Alto group; PK/PD modeling, EEG/BIS measures of drug effect, and anesthetic drug interactions (later Hospital Clínic de Barcelona)

Gambús specializes in the quantitative pharmacodynamics of anesthetic and analgesic drugs, using processed-EEG measures (including bispectral/EEG-derived endpoints) to characterize the time course of drug effect and to model the effect-site equilibration (ke0) that underlies effect-site targeting in TCI. His research addresses propofol and opioid pharmacodynamics and their synergistic interactions, an area central to how modern TCI systems combine hypnotic and opioid targets.

He is a co-author of the landmark Schnider propofol study, developed during his time in the Stanford/Palo Alto research group of Steven Shafer and Donald Stanski (with Thomas Schnider and Charles Minto) — the study that produced the widely deployed "Schnider" propofol TCI model incorporating a ke0 derived from an EEG measure of effect. He subsequently led a PK/PD research program at the Hospital Clínic de Barcelona.

*Key reference:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, Andresen C, Goodale DB, Shafer SL, Youngs EJ. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182.

**Keith M. Gregg** — engineer/scientist, Stanford University Department of Anesthesia; effect-site TCI control algorithms

Keith M. Gregg collaborated with Steven L. Shafer at Stanford on the mathematics and control algorithms underpinning effect-site target-controlled infusion (TCI). With Shafer he co-authored the foundational paper describing how a computer-controlled infusion pump can be driven to reach and then hold a target concentration at the site of drug effect rather than in plasma. That work formalized the algorithms — built on the plasma–effect-site rate constant ke0 and the closed-form three-compartment model — for computing the sequence of infusion rates that produces the most rapid, non-overshooting approach to a specified effect-site target, and then maintains it. These algorithms became the effect-site targeting logic implemented in STANPUMP and, in turn, the conceptual basis for the effect-site (ke0) targeting that stanpumpR reproduces.

Gregg also contributed to the anesthetic drug-interaction literature as a co-author of the Minto response-surface model, which extended single-drug concentration–response relationships to a mathematically consistent surface describing hypnotic and opioid interactions (e.g., propofol with opioids) — the same class of response-surface interaction modeling reflected in stanpumpR's interaction facet.

*Key references:* Shafer SL, Gregg KM. Algorithms to rapidly achieve and maintain stable drug concentrations at the site of drug effect with a computer-controlled infusion pump. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(2):147–169. • Minto CF, Schnider TW, Short TG, Gregg KM, Gentilini A, Shafer SL. Response surface model for anesthetic drug interactions. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(6):1603–1616.

**Chuanpu Hu** — pharmacometrician/statistician; PhD Stanford University; postdoctoral fellow, Stanford Department of Anesthesia (later industry pharmacometrics)

Chuanpu Hu earned his PhD at Stanford and worked with Steven L. Shafer's group in the Stanford Department of Anesthesia (postdoctoral fellowship in clinical pharmacology, mid-1990s) on the statistical and control-theoretic methodology of PK/PD modeling for anesthetic drugs. With Shafer and William S. Lovejoy he analyzed control strategies for the three-compartment PK/PD models that describe intravenous anesthetics, comparing algorithmic approaches for driving plasma and effect-site concentrations to target — work directly relevant to the optimization and effect-site targeting logic used in target-controlled infusion.

Hu subsequently built a long career in pharmacometrics in the pharmaceutical industry, including senior scientific and directorial roles at Johnson & Johnson/Janssen and Bristol Myers Squibb (and, earlier, a period as a mathematical statistician at the FDA). His industry work centers on population PK/PD analysis, nonlinear mixed-effects modeling, exposure–response methodology, and simulation — the statistical toolkit that population anesthetic PK/PD models such as those in stanpumpR rely upon.

*Key reference:* Hu C, Lovejoy WS, Shafer SL. Comparison of some control strategies for three-compartment PK/PD models. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1994;22(6):525–550.

**Charles F. Minto** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician; research fellow with Steven Shafer at Stanford; co-developer of the remifentanil (Minto) model and of response-surface interaction modeling (later based in Sydney, Australia)

Minto, during his research fellowship at Stanford in Steven Shafer's laboratory (with Thomas Schnider), developed the population pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for remifentanil that bears his name and remains a standard model in target-controlled infusion (TCI) systems. The model characterized how age and lean body mass shift remifentanil disposition and effect, and introduced an age-dependent effect-site equilibration rate constant (ke0) linking plasma concentration to EEG effect. He later formalized the mathematics of anesthetic drug interactions, proposing a response-surface framework that extends single-drug sigmoid concentration–response relationships to combinations (e.g., propofol–opioid), which underlies the interaction modeling used in modern anesthesia simulation. Minto subsequently practiced in Sydney, Australia, and co-founded the Open TCI Initiative with Schnider.

*Key references:* Minto CF, Schnider TW, Egan TD, et al. Influence of age and gender on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of remifentanil. I. Model development. Anesthesiology. 1997;86(1):10–23. • Minto CF, Schnider TW, Short TG, Gregg KM, Gentilini A, Shafer SL. Response surface model for anesthetic drug interactions. Anesthesiology. 2000;92(6):1603–1616.

**Thomas W. Schnider** — anesthesiologist; research fellow with Steven Shafer at Stanford; developer of the Schnider propofol PK/PD model widely used for TCI (later head of the Institute for Anaesthesiology, Kantonsspital St. Gallen, Switzerland)

Schnider, during his research fellowship at Stanford in Steven Shafer's laboratory (with Charles Minto), derived the covariate-based propofol pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models that are among the most widely implemented in commercial effect-site TCI pumps. The pharmacokinetic study defined how method of administration and covariates (age, weight, height, lean body mass) influence propofol disposition, and the companion pharmacodynamic study quantified the influence of age on propofol effect and on the plasma–effect-site equilibration constant (ke0), enabling effect-site targeting. He later became head of the Institute for Anaesthesiology at Kantonsspital St. Gallen, Switzerland, and co-founded the Open TCI Initiative with Minto.

*Key references:* Schnider TW, Minto CF, Gambus PL, et al. The influence of method of administration and covariates on the pharmacokinetics of propofol in adult volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1998;88(5):1170–1182. • Schnider TW, Minto CF, Shafer SL, et al. The influence of age on propofol pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 1999;90(6):1502–1516.

**Steven L. Shafer** — anesthesiologist and pharmacologist; author of stanpumpR and the original STANPUMP infusion program; Professor of Anesthesiology, Perioperative and Pain Medicine

Steven Shafer is known for translating anesthetic PK/PD theory into working drug-delivery tools. In the late 1980s he wrote STANPUMP (Stanford Pump), a computer program that drove infusion pumps to achieve and maintain user-specified plasma or effect-site concentrations of intravenous anesthetics — an implementation of target-controlled infusion (TCI) built on closed-form solutions to multi-compartment models. With Keith Gregg, he published the control algorithms for rapidly achieving and maintaining stable effect-site concentrations, extending TCI from plasma targeting to effect-site targeting using the ke0 parameter. stanpumpR is his open-source R/Shiny successor to this line of work, using the same closed-form compartmental mathematics to simulate plasma and effect-site concentrations.

Shafer's research spans opioid and hypnotic pharmacology, population modeling, and the pharmacokinetic concepts clinicians use to reason about infusion regimens — including context-sensitive decrement times and rational drug selection based on predicted concentration trajectories. He has also been influential in research integrity and publication ethics, including a long tenure as Editor-in-Chief of Anesthesia & Analgesia.

*Key references:* Shafer SL, Gregg KM. Algorithms to rapidly achieve and maintain stable drug concentrations at the site of drug effect with a computer-controlled infusion pump. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(2):147–169. • Shafer SL, Varvel JR. Pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and rational opioid selection. Anesthesiology. 1991;74(1):53–63.

**Donald R. Stanski** — anesthesiologist and clinical pharmacologist, Professor (Emeritus) of Anesthesia

Donald Stanski helped establish the rigorous, model-based study of intravenous anesthetic drugs. A recurring theme of his work is the use of the processed electroencephalogram (EEG) as a continuous, quantifiable measure of anesthetic drug effect, allowing pharmacodynamics to be modeled with the same precision as pharmacokinetics. His collaboration with Lewis Sheiner produced the effect-compartment model (see California/UCSF), linking plasma concentration to drug effect through ke0 and providing the conceptual basis for effect-site targeting.

Stanski applied population PK/PD methods (NONMEM) to the anesthetic agents themselves, notably thiopental, fentanyl, and alfentanil, quantifying how advancing age reduces dose requirements through pharmacodynamic rather than purely pharmacokinetic mechanisms. His mentorship and collaboration at Stanford — including work with Steven Shafer on computer-controlled infusion — connected quantitative pharmacology to bedside drug delivery, and he later carried these principles into pharmaceutical drug development and regulatory science.

*Key reference:* Stanski DR, Maitre PO. Population pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of thiopental: the effect of age revisited. Anesthesiology. 1990;72(3):412–422.

**John R. Varvel** — anesthesiologist; developer of standardized performance metrics for computer-controlled infusion pumps `[verify: Stanford affiliation]`

John Varvel, working with Steven L. Shafer, addressed a foundational methodological problem in target-controlled infusion: how to quantify, in a statistically sound and clinically interpretable way, how well a computer-controlled infusion pump achieves its target concentrations. Their 1992 paper defined a now-standard set of performance measures based on the performance error between predicted and measured drug concentrations — median performance error (MDPE, a measure of bias), median absolute performance error (MDAPE, a measure of inaccuracy), divergence (drift over time), and wobble (intra-individual variability).

These four metrics became the accepted vocabulary for validating and comparing pharmacokinetic models and TCI devices, and they remain the reporting standard in prospective TCI model-validation studies today.

*Key reference:* Varvel JR, Donoho DL, Shafer SL. Measuring the predictive performance of computer-controlled infusion pumps. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1992;20(1):63–94.

**Russell D. Wada** — pharmacometrician; physiologic/recirculatory PK modeling of anesthetics and population PK (Stanford Dept. of Anesthesia during the anesthesia-modeling era; later Pharsight/Certara)

Russ Wada received his PhD from UCLA (1991) and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Stanford University in Donald Stanski's anesthesia pharmacology group, working with William F. Ebling, followed by roughly four years as a research associate in the Stanford Department of Anesthesia `[verify: duration]`. In that period he developed physiologically based and recirculatory pharmacokinetic models of intravenous anesthetics — most notably thiopental — that describe drug behavior in terms of tissue blood flows, tissue masses, and organ clearances rather than abstract compartments. This physiologic framing captures the first-pass and early-distribution phase that governs the rapid rise and fall of anesthetic concentrations after an IV bolus, and it allowed simulation of how altered cardiac output and body composition change thiopental disposition. His work connected to the broader recirculatory-modeling community, including the Northwestern group (Krejcie, Avram, Henthorn).

After academia, Wada moved into pharmacometrics consulting, joining Pharsight Corporation (later part of Certara) in 1997 and subsequently Certara/Quantitative Solutions, and more recently QuanTx Consulting, becoming a recognized leader in model-based drug development across many therapeutic areas.

*Key reference:* Wada DR, Björkman S, Ebling WF, Harashima H, Harapat SR, Stanski DR. Computer simulation of the effects of alterations in blood flows and body composition on thiopental pharmacokinetics in humans. Anesthesiology. 1997;87(4):884–899.

## Stellenbosch University (South Africa)

**Johan F. Coetzee** — anesthesiologist; Emeritus Professor, Department of Anaesthesiology and Critical Care `[verify: emeritus status]`

Coetzee is known for rigorous clinical evaluation of propofol pharmacokinetic parameter sets for target-controlled infusion. His widely cited comparison of three propofol PK parameter sets (Marsh, Tackley, and Dyck) driving TCI in the same patients quantified the bias and inaccuracy each model introduced into predicted plasma concentrations, informing model selection for propofol TCI systems. His broader research includes pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in cardiac anesthesia and the clinical application of TCI.

*Key reference:* Coetzee JF, Glen JB, Wium CA, Boshoff L. Pharmacokinetic model selection for target controlled infusions of propofol: assessment of three parameter sets. Anesthesiology. 1995;82(6):1328–1345.

## Universidad Católica & Universidad de Chile (Santiago / Viña del Mar)

**Luis Ignacio Cortínez** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; population PK/PD, TCI, and allometric scaling

Cortínez is a leading figure in the Latin-American TCI/PK community and an internationally recognized population pharmacokineticist. His work applies nonlinear mixed-effects modeling and theory-based allometric scaling — using fat-free mass and normal fat mass as size descriptors — to explain how body weight and composition alter drug disposition, with particular attention to obesity. He has built and evaluated population models for dexmedetomidine, ketamine, and propofol, and has contributed extensively to the methodology of covariate scaling in anesthetic PK.

He collaborates closely with pharmacometricians such as Brian J. Anderson and Nick Holford, and with the Chilean anesthesia group including Pablo Sepúlveda. His obesity-focused models are widely cited in guidance on dosing anesthetics and sedatives in obese patients.

**Pablo O. Sepúlveda** — anesthesiologist, Chile (Viña del Mar `[verify: primary institution]`); propofol TCI, effect-site pharmacodynamics, and ke0 estimation

Sepúlveda is a Chilean anesthesiologist known for critical, clinically grounded investigation of effect-site (ke0) modeling in propofol TCI. His work examines how the plasma–effect-site equilibration rate constant behaves under different infusion speeds and how age influences effect-site targeting, and he has argued for careful re-evaluation of the effect-site model as implemented in propofol PK/PD models (including the Eleveld model). This line of work bears directly on how TCI pumps translate a target concentration into loss and recovery of consciousness.

He collaborates with Luis Ignacio Cortínez and other members of the Chilean PK/PD community, contributing to the Latin-American body of TCI research and to ongoing debate over the correct parameterization of propofol effect-site kinetics.

## University Medical Center Groningen (Netherlands)

**Anthony R. Absalom** — anesthesiologist; Professor of Anesthesiology, UMC Groningen

Absalom is a leading investigator in TCI, closed-loop anesthesia, and propofol/remifentanil clinical pharmacology. Early in his career at Glasgow (with Gavin Kenny) he reported closed-loop control of propofol anesthesia using the Bispectral Index as the feedback variable, and he was closely involved in the "Paedfusor," a pediatric propofol TCI system incorporating a child-specific pharmacokinetic data set, whose accuracy he evaluated in children undergoing cardiac surgery or catheterization. At Groningen he has collaborated closely with Michel Struys.

Absalom co-authored (with Douglas Eleveld and Struys) the Eleveld "general-purpose" propofol PK/PD model, developed to apply across broad populations from children to the elderly and now widely implemented in TCI devices. He is also a prolific author and editor of the TCI and intravenous-anesthesia literature.

*Key references:* Absalom AR, Sutcliffe N, Kenny GN. Closed-loop control of anesthesia using Bispectral index: performance assessment in patients undergoing major orthopedic surgery under combined general and regional anesthesia. Anesthesiology. 2002;96(1):67–73. • Eleveld DJ, Colin P, Absalom AR, Struys MMRF. Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for propofol for broad application in anaesthesia and sedation. Br J Anaesth. 2018;120(5):942–959.

**Douglas J. Eleveld** — pharmacometrician; general-purpose ("Eleveld") propofol and remifentanil PK/PD models spanning all ages

Eleveld, with Michel Struys, Anthony Absalom, and colleagues at Groningen, developed general-purpose ("all-in-one") pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic models intended to apply across the entire patient spectrum — from neonates to the elderly, and from underweight to morbidly obese — rather than being restricted to a narrow population. His propofol PK/PD model, built by pooling data from many prior studies and using bispectral index (BIS) as the effect endpoint, and his allometric remifentanil model, using age, weight, and sex as covariates, have been increasingly adopted in modern TCI systems as unified alternatives to the older Marsh, Schnider, and Minto models. These models incorporate effect-site (ke0) parameterization for effect-site–targeted infusion.

*Key references:* Eleveld DJ, Colin P, Absalom AR, Struys MMRF. Pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic model for propofol for broad application in anaesthesia and sedation. Br J Anaesth. 2018;120(5):942–959. • Eleveld DJ, Proost JH, Vereecke H, et al. An allometric model of remifentanil pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Anesthesiology. 2017;126(6):1005–1018.

**Michel M. R. F. Struys** — anesthesiologist; Professor and Chair of Anesthesiology, UMC Groningen, and Ghent University (Belgium)

Struys is a central figure in the development and clinical validation of target-controlled infusion (TCI) and automated ("closed-loop") anesthesia. Working at Ghent University with biomedical engineer Tom De Smet, he co-developed the RUGLOOP TCI and closed-loop research software and reported one of the first patient-individualized, model-based, adaptive closed-loop systems that used the Bispectral Index (BIS) as the controlled variable to titrate propofol. His group's work spans effect-site (Ce) targeting, characterization of propofol pharmacodynamics and drug interactions, and comparative evaluation of infusion strategies against manual control.

His later collaborations extended this line of work to Bayesian, patient-adaptive controllers and to combined propofol–remifentanil closed-loop coadministration. After moving to Groningen he continued as a leading investigator in TCI and closed-loop control, frequently publishing alongside Anthony Absalom, and contributed to development and validation of general-purpose propofol PK/PD models used in modern TCI.

*Key reference:* Struys MMRF, De Smet T, Versichelen LFM, Van de Velde S, Van den Broecke R, Mortier EP. Comparison of closed-loop controlled administration of propofol using Bispectral Index as the controlled variable versus "standard practice" controlled administration. Anesthesiology. 2001;95(1):6–17.

## University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)

**Stuart L. Beal** — biostatistician; co-developer of NONMEM and nonlinear mixed-effects (population) pharmacokinetics

Stuart Beal earned his PhD in biostatistics from UCLA (1973) and spent his career as a professor of biostatistics at UCSF, where his decades-long partnership with clinical pharmacologist Lewis B. Sheiner produced the population approach to pharmacokinetics and its enduring software embodiment, NONMEM (NONlinear Mixed Effects Modeling). The Beal–Sheiner framework treats sparse, unbalanced clinical data from many subjects as a single analysis, simultaneously estimating typical (fixed-effect) parameter values, their covariate dependencies, and the random inter-individual and residual variability. This reframing — modeling the population rather than fitting each patient separately — became the methodological foundation of modern pharmacometrics and model-informed drug development.

Beal was primarily responsible for the statistical estimation machinery underlying NONMEM, including the first-order (FO) method and, later, the first-order conditional estimation (FOCE) methods that improved accuracy when data are informative about individual parameters. His authorship of the successive NONMEM Users Guides made these estimation algorithms usable across pharmacology and industry, where NONMEM remains a de facto standard. In anesthesia, the population approach he and Sheiner established underpins the covariate-based PK models and TCI parameter sets used to dose intravenous anesthetics and opioids. Stuart Beal passed away in 2006.

*Key references:* Beal SL, Sheiner LB. Estimating population kinetics. Crit Rev Biomed Eng. 1982;8(3):195–222. • Beal SL, Sheiner LB, eds. NONMEM Users Guides. San Francisco: NONMEM Project Group, University of California, San Francisco.

---

**Edmund I. "Ted" Eger II** — anesthesiologist and inhaled-anesthetic pharmacologist; originator of the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) standard

Ted Eger was the defining figure in the pharmacology of inhaled (volatile) anesthetics. Joining the UCSF faculty in 1960, he originated and standardized the concept of Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) — the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic, at one atmosphere, that prevents movement in response to a noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects. MAC became, and remains, the universal measure of inhaled-anesthetic potency and the common currency for comparing agents and dosing them clinically.

Beyond potency, Eger characterized the uptake, distribution, and elimination kinetics of volatile anesthetics — how factors such as blood:gas and tissue solubility, ventilation, and cardiac output govern the speed of anesthetic onset and recovery. He applied this framework to the early human pharmacology of successive agents including halothane, isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane, publishing more than 500 peer-reviewed papers over his career. The MAC concept was developed with UCSF colleagues Lawrence J. Saidman and Bernard Brandstater. Ted Eger passed away in 2017.

*Key reference:* Eger EI II, Saidman LJ, Brandstater B. Minimum alveolar anesthetic concentration: a standard of anesthetic potency. Anesthesiology. 1965;26(6):756–763.

---

**Dennis M. Fisher** — anesthesiologist and pharmacometrician, Professor Emeritus of Anesthesia

Dennis Fisher is a clinical pharmacologist recognized for methodological rigor in anesthetic PK/PD analysis and for extending compartmental modeling into pediatric anesthesia. Much of his work characterized the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of neuromuscular blocking drugs — including vecuronium, atracurium, and pancuronium — across the age spectrum from neonates to adults, clarifying how developmental changes in body composition and clearance alter dosing. His analyses of atracurium elimination quantified the relative contributions of Hofmann degradation, ester hydrolysis, and organ-based clearance.

Fisher used PK/PD simulation to explain clinically important but counterintuitive phenomena — for example, why recovery time lengthens disproportionately after larger or repeated relaxant doses — demonstrating how the interaction of pharmacokinetics with a sigmoid concentration-effect relationship shapes the observed time course of drug effect. Beyond his own studies, he served as a reviewer at the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, an editor at Anesthesiology, and a widely cited educator on statistical and pharmacometric methods in anesthesia research.

*Key references:* Fisher DM, Rosen JI. A pharmacokinetic explanation for increasing recovery time following larger or repeated doses of nondepolarizing muscle relaxants. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(3):286–291. • Fisher DM, Canfell PC, Fahey MR, et al. Elimination of atracurium in humans: contribution of Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis versus organ-based elimination. Anesthesiology. 1986;65(1):6–12.

---

**Lewis B. Sheiner** — physician-pharmacologist; co-founder of population pharmacokinetics and pharmacometrics

Lewis Sheiner was a foundational figure in quantitative clinical pharmacology whose methods underlie essentially all modern anesthetic PK/PD modeling. With statistician Stuart L. Beal at UCSF, he developed the nonlinear mixed-effects modeling framework and its software implementation, NONMEM, which made it possible to estimate population pharmacokinetic parameters — and the between-subject and residual variability around them — from sparse, routinely collected clinical data rather than dense experimental sampling. This "population approach" became the standard for characterizing how covariates such as age, weight, and organ function shift drug disposition, and it is the statistical engine behind the population models stanpumpR uses.

In anesthesia specifically, Sheiner's collaboration with Donald Stanski produced the effect-compartment (link) model, introduced in their analysis of d-tubocurarine. By positing a hypothetical effect site connected to plasma by a first-order rate constant (ke0), they explained the temporal lag (hysteresis) between plasma concentration and observed drug effect, and made it possible to fit pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics simultaneously. The effect-site concentration and ke0 concepts that this work established are precisely what target-controlled infusion systems and stanpumpR simulate. Sheiner also shaped drug-development methodology more broadly, articulating the distinction between "learning" and "confirming" trials. He received the ASCPT Oscar B. Hunter Award in 2004. Lewis Sheiner passed away in 2004.

*Key references:* Sheiner LB, Stanski DR, Vozeh S, Miller RD, Ham J. Simultaneous modeling of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics: application to d-tubocurarine. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 1979;25(3):358–371. • Sheiner LB, Beal SL. Evaluation of methods for estimating population pharmacokinetic parameters. I. Michaelis-Menten model: routine clinical pharmacokinetic data. J Pharmacokinet Biopharm. 1980;8(6):553–571. `[verify: volume/issue/pages]`

## University of Glasgow

**Gavin N. C. Kenny** — anesthesiologist; co-developer of the "Diprifusor" commercial TCI system and clinical implementer of the Marsh propofol model

Kenny, Professor of Anaesthesia at the University of Glasgow, pioneered the clinical application of computer-controlled drug delivery, targeting a drug's concentration in the patient rather than merely its infusion rate. With Martin White he built a computerized propofol infusion system, and the underlying pharmacokinetic model — published with Brian Marsh and Neil Morton — became known as the Marsh model, a weight-proportional adaptation of the Gepts parameter set that remains pre-programmed in many TCI pumps. His research directly enabled the "Diprifusor," the first commercially available TCI system for propofol, launched by Zeneca/AstraZeneca in 1996.

*Key reference:* Marsh B, White M, Morton N, Kenny GNC. Pharmacokinetic model driven infusion of propofol in children. Br J Anaesth. 1991;67(1):41–48.

## University of Utah

**Talmage D. Egan** — anesthesiologist; remifentanil pharmacology, obesity PK, and novel opioids

Egan is a leading investigator in intravenous anesthetic pharmacology and total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA), best known for foundational clinical pharmacology of remifentanil, including its first human pharmacokinetic characterization and studies of its disposition in obesity. He co-authored the original remifentanil model-development work with Minto, Schnider, and Shafer, and later led development of a population pharmacokinetic model incorporating body mass to guide remifentanil dosing across the range from lean to obese patients. His work spans anesthetic drug interaction, pharmacokinetic modeling for TCI, and the preclinical/translational pharmacology of newer "soft" and novel opioids. He is Professor and served as Chair of Anesthesiology at the University of Utah School of Medicine.

*Key references:* Egan TD, Lemmens HJ, Fiset P, et al. The pharmacokinetics of the new short-acting opioid remifentanil (GI87084B) in healthy adult male volunteers. Anesthesiology. 1993;79(5):881–892. `[verify: volume/pages]` • Kim TK, Obara S, Egan TD, et al. Disposition of remifentanil in obesity: a new pharmacokinetic model incorporating the influence of body mass. Anesthesiology. 2017;126(6):1019–1032.

**Steven E. Kern** — engineer and pharmaceutical scientist, University of Utah (Pharmaceutics, Anesthesiology, and Bioengineering); opioid–hypnotic interaction and model-based delivery (later the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation)

Steven Kern is a bioengineer and clinical pharmacologist who spent roughly fifteen years on the faculty at the University of Utah, with appointments spanning Pharmaceutics, Anesthesiology, and Bioengineering. Trained in engineering (mechanical engineering, Cornell; bioengineering, Penn State and Utah), he applied a strongly quantitative, model-based approach to anesthetic PK/PD, working alongside the Utah anesthesia group — notably Talmage D. Egan and, in closed-loop/model-based delivery work, Dwayne Westenskow. His research emphasized effect-site modeling, opioid–hypnotic synergy, and the translation of interaction models into model-based and closed-loop drug delivery.

Kern is best known in this area for a volunteer study, published back-to-back with Bouillon's paper in the same 2004 issue of Anesthesiology, that used a response surface to characterize the propofol–remifentanil pharmacodynamic interaction across a complete range of clinically relevant concentrations. Using surrogate noxious stimuli (algometry, tetany), sedation, and laryngoscopy as endpoints, the analysis quantified pronounced synergy between the two drugs, reinforcing the rationale for combining a hypnotic and an opioid at reduced individual concentrations. He later moved into industry (pharmacology modeling, including at Novartis, Basel) and then to global health, serving in quantitative-sciences leadership at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. `[verify: birth year; exact Utah and Novartis dates]`

*Key reference:* Kern SE, Xie G, White JL, Egan TD. A response surface analysis of propofol–remifentanil pharmacodynamic interaction in volunteers. Anesthesiology. 2004;100(6):1373–1381.

**Dwayne R. Westenskow** — bioengineer; professor of anesthesiology and bioengineering; automated (closed-loop) drug delivery, anesthesia monitoring, and patient safety

Westenskow built one of the longest-running academic programs in automated anesthesia delivery and monitoring. Beginning in the 1970s with oxygen-consumption measurement during anesthesia, he turned to feedback control in 1977 and, over the following decades, demonstrated closed-loop controllers for volatile-anesthetic and respiratory-gas delivery, blood pressure (e.g., nitroprusside infusion), neuromuscular blockade, mechanical ventilation, and fluid resuscitation — showing that automatic controllers could match expert clinicians. His group integrated these controllers into the concept of an automated "anesthesia workstation," and he made major contributions to intelligent alarms, artificial-neural-network signal processing, and noninvasive monitoring (including CO2-rebreathing cardiac output). Much of this work connects the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modeling of anesthetics to the engineering of the sensors and controllers needed to deliver them safely in real time.

*Key reference:* Westenskow DR, Wallroth CF. Closed-loop control for anesthesia breathing systems. J Clin Monit. 1990;6(3):249–256. `[verify: issue number]`
